# The 2026 overbuild (generated by tools/overbuild_2026.py)

2026 consents (last_12_months, observed only): 40,908; 2026 building = 0.95 x consents = 38,863 dwellings (all categories).
Requirement 2026 22,103 -> excess +16,760; requirement 2027 28,889 -> gap_ref +9,974 (basis 2027), fading at rho = 0.52.
Booked as surplus: market excess +27,479, absorbed -27,479, net +0 dwellings over 2026-2050 (variant REF; absorbed by 2035).
Implied vacancy (1 - households / (stock + surplus still vacant)): peak 6.33% in 2028, 5.39% in 2050 (the vacancy-rate parameter: its published 2023 census value, 5.39%); census 1986-2023 range 5.08-8.09% (empty dwellings; before 2013 the empty share of unoccupied is estimated, and 2013->2018 is a definitional break).
Consistent definition (pooled 2018/2023 empty share of unoccupied, 49.2%): 1986 4.42%, 1991 4.64%, 1996 4.01%, 2001 4.81%, 2006 4.80%, 2013 5.22%, 2018 5.08%, 2023 5.38%.
Sensitivity, booked as redevelopment: implied net removals peak at 23,041 in 2026 (default: 6,281).

Limitation: The vacancy-rate parameter is held at its published 2023 census value (5.39%; on the consistent definition 2023 is the series maximum, 5.38%, minimum 4.01% in 1996); the 2026 overbuild raises implied stock vacancy temporarily and is absorbed by 2035, so implied vacancy returns to the parameter (5.39% in 2050). The 2026 overbuild (market excess ≈27,500 dwellings over 2026-2050, of which ≈24,600 in 2026-2028) is absorbed by 2035 along the normalised logistic of the levers (≈27,500 dwellings built less; implied vacancy peaks at 6.33% in 2028). Stock-flow theory of the housing market (Rosen & Smith 1983; Wheaton 1990; DiPasquale & Wheaton 1992; Gabriel & Nothaft 2001) fixes the direction, reversion of vacancy to its equilibrium rate, not the speed; 2035 is the common RECC adoption window of the model and the speed is bracketed by sensitivity rows (never absorbed, by 2030, by 2045). The persistence rho = 0.52 describes how the flow deviation fades, not the payback of the stock.
